# Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 61 (Bu-Vb Pc61)

**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** 61. Intentionally killing a living being

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 61 (titled *Sañcicca*) defines the ecclesiastical offense incurred when a monk intentionally deprives an animal of life (*yo pana bhikkhu sañcicca pāṇaṁ jīvitā voropeyya, pācittiyaṁ*) [SuttaCentral; Bechert 1992; Buddhism into the Year 2000]. The rule requires confession for killing a living being intentionally [SuttaCentral]. The introductory narrative setting for the rule features the shooting of crows [Schmithausen 1991b]. In the legal terminology of the Vinaya, *pāṇa* here specifically designates animals, contrasting with human beings—whose intentional killing entails permanent expulsion under Pārājika 3—and with plants or seeds, the destruction of which is addressed separately under Pācittiya 11 [Buddhism into the Year 2000; Schmithausen 1991a; Collins 1993; Schmithausen 2009; Schmithausen 1991b]. The internal Vibhaṅga casuistry details five legal permutations based on perception and doubt: killing an animal while consciously aware that it is an animal incurs a *pācittiya*; doing so while in doubt incurs a *dukkaṭa*; killing an animal while mistaking it for an inanimate object incurs no offense (*anāpatti*); and acting toward a non-animal while mistaking it for an animal or doubting it incurs a *dukkaṭa* [Stache-Rosen 1984; Sujato 2011].

SuttaCentral identifies direct parallels to this rule across the extant Vinayas of other early Buddhist schools, including the Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, and Mahāsāṅghika traditions preserved in Chinese, Sanskrit, and Tibetan, alongside the parallel nun's rule (Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 142) [SuttaCentral]. In some non-Pali versions of the rule, the term *pāṇa* is explicitly glossed as animals (*tiryagyonigata*) [Schmithausen 1991b]. DharmaNexus detects 323 Pali-internal text-reuse matches across 78 texts, sharing extensive formulaic legal phrases with rules such as Pācittiya 45, Pācittiya 30, Saṅghādisesa 5, and Pārājika 3, as well as automatic cross-language alignments with the Tibetan *Vinayavibhaṅga* (D0003-3) and *Pratimokṣasūtravṛtti* (D4107) [DharmaNexus]. An English translation has been prepared by Bhikkhu Brahmali [SuttaCentral].
